newsitem.title: UK: BAe investors nervous after Labour victory.
newsitem.headline: BAe investors nervous after Labour victory.

text.p: A bearish attack on British Aerospace shares this week have thrown up a host of reasons for the selloff, but fears about the new Labour government's policy on defence could be encouraging investors to take some profits, analysts said.
The shares were down on Wednesday a further 11-1/2 pence at 1274p against a rising market, extending the steady fall from 1352 pence over the last seven days.
Some analysts said an impending defence review by Labour and reports that foreign minister Robin Cook planned to tighten up restrictions on arms exports was overshadowing the stock.
"We don't know what that means or where BAe stands in terms of the review process but it is bound to cause concern," said one analyst.
Government officials told reporters on Tuesday that Cook intends to take a much closer look at firms that wish to export arms to "sensitive" countries.
"One major new thread in government policy will be the application of human rights," one official said.
"This is at the centre of policy and will have a good deal of relevance in new procedures to be set up on defence exports and so on."

Cook has already backed the idea of a Europe-wide code of conduct on arms sales, saying Britain has the right to maintain its competitive edge in the arms market but must also accept responsibility to ensure that market is properly regulated.
"No individual countries have been scrutinised yet but each application (to export defence equipment) will be looked at very closely in the case of sensitive countries," the official said.
More details should become clear during an upcoming parliamentary debate on foreign affairs.

But other analysts blamed BAe's share price fall on resurgent fears that Germany would pull out of the Eurofighter 2000 aircraft project and that Airbus Industrie partners are arguing over their plans to convert the four-nation cooperative into a company.

There were also reports in the market of concerns that U.S. rival Boeing Co posted disappointing first-quarter results last week and that there were concerns BAe might lose out in the international scramble to get a part of France's soon to be privatised defence electronics to missiles giant Thomson CSF.

But what was not in doubt was that one of the British share market's top performers was suffering an old-fashioned bout of profit-taking after the share hit an all-time closing high of 1371 on March 11, up 61 percent or 524p on a year ago.
"There are numerous stories," said Brian Newman at institutional brokers Henderson Crosthwaite.

"There are four or five different versions -- it starts with Boeing first-quarter profits, then there's Eurofighter, then there's export licnences, then there's Airbus disputes and then there's French (industry) consolidation," he said.
But his favoured diagnosis was tantamount to saying there were more sellers than buyers. "I just think the stock's come down because it's gone up...There are instances when that's the case," he said.
"I think it is purely technical in the marketplace. There have been a few sellers and the marketmakers have got stock," he added.
